27.21.2.en: * They must know, for example, that the holy sayings are fulfilled in them when it cries out: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Prov 27:22). And the prophet complains of them, saying: “Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction” (Jer 5:3). Therefore the Lord also said: “I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways” (Jer 15:7). He also says: “For the people turneth not unto him that smiteth them” (Isa 9:13), and again the prophet complains in the voice of those who are admonished by the wounds of sufferings: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed” (Jer 51:9); the remedy was offered to Babylon, but she was not healed. This is because the soul, when it hears words of rebuke and feels the pains they cause while it is in the depths of committing iniquity, does not care and does not return to the straight way of salvation. Thus the Lord rebuked the people of Israel while they were in captivity and had not turned from the way of iniquity, saying: “The house of Israel is to me become dross: all they are brass, and tin, and iron, and lead, in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek 22:18). This means in truth that God willed to purify them in the fire of His wrath and sufferings, to make them gold or silver, but “they have gone far from me, and have become brass and tin and iron and lead, yet even in the midst of trials they ventured, not upon virtue, but upon doing vice.

27.21.3.en: Brass resounds with a louder noise than any other metal when we strike it. Therefore when a man is purified he makes noises, as though he had become brass in the midst of the furnace.

27.21.4.en: And when tin is skillfully treated, it falsely appears as silver. Therefore those who have not abandoned the vice of love of display while in the midst of sufferings have become tin in the furnace.

27.21.5.en: Likewise a man uses iron in the furnace when he harms his brethren and neighbors even while in the midst of torments.

27.21.6.en: As for lead, it is the heaviest of metals; therefore those who are weighed down with the load of sins, and whom even sufferings have not been able to keep away from earthly lusts, have become as lead in the furnace. For this reason it is written by the prophet Ezekiel: “She hath wearied herself with toils, and her great rust went not forth out of her; her rust is in the fire” (Ezek 24:12).

27.21.7.en: God sends upon us the fire of judgment to cleanse us from the rust (corrosion) of iniquity and vices. The rust did not come out even by the fire, because we, in the midst of afflictions and sufferings, did not shake off vices from ourselves. Therefore the prophet also says: “The founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them” (Jer 6:29-30).

27.21.8.en: Let us realize, however, that those whom afflictions do not drive to reform may have their fear calmed by gentle sermons full of love. And those whom sufferings do not reform in their correction may be turned away from doing evil by gentle indulgence. As is well known, a sick man may not be healed by strong doses of medicines, while often lukewarm water alone restores him to his natural condition. Likewise some wounds which are not healed by operations of excision are healed by a little dressing with oil. And in the same way the strong diamond is not cut by steel at all, but the blood of goats may soften it.

27.22.0.en: Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds [23].

27.22.1.en: He who relies on his wealth and riches does not care about his flock of sheep, yet wealth passes away and honor comes to an end, and even kings are exposed to falling, so he returns to his flock to find it scattered. Therefore it is fitting for a man, however great his wealth and whatever authority he has obtained, to be diligent in caring for his flock, for this is good for the flock as well as for himself.

27.22.2.en: Many of the rich and the nobles were lazy and slack, relying on their money and positions, and leaving the management of their affairs in the hands of others without concern on their part.

27.22.3.en: * It is not fitting to address simply to all who have believed in Christ teachings on every point, for it is written: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks.” For the way is very different from one person to another: this one begins in the paths of truth in order to become a disciple, and that one is established in his mind and able to understand the height and the depth and the length and the breadth. With the first use simple teaching in which there is no difficulty of understanding and which does not need deep thought. Advise him to flee from the errors of polytheism, and urge him to discern the beauty of the creatures and the Creator and Maker of creation.

27.23.0.en: St. Cyril the Great For riches are not for ever: and doth the crown endure to every generation? [24].

27.23.1.en: Since the wise man asks even the rich and the great to work and be diligent, so that they care for their flocks of sheep and manage their affairs well, he assures them not to rely on their money and their wealth and their authority, even the crown of the king. All these are liable to loss, for a man’s capital is his striving and care, not his wealth and position.

27.23.2.en: The scholar Tertullian spoke with some elaboration in order to answer the accusation brought against the Christians that they are idle and unproductive. He also affirms that the Christians share with the pagans in practicing all occupations, and do not despise any profession unless it corrupts the spiritual life.

27.23.3.en: * For we remember that we ought to be thankful to the Lord our God and Creator. We reject no fruit of His works; we use them with moderation and not with mistaken extremism. Therefore we do not fail to frequent the public squares and markets and baths and shops and factories and inns and all your occupations, and to have all the other relationships so that we may express our life with you in this world. With you we sail the sea, and enlist in military service, and till the earth and trade, and we sell openly the products of our trade and manufactures that you use.

27.23.4.en: Tertullian Origen says that no one is idle in the house of the wise man.

27.24.0.en: The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered [25].

27.24.1.en: The wise man calls the shepherds to provide food for their flocks, for the hay is gone, that is, it has been cut from the earth to be provided as food, and the grass has appeared, and the herbs of the mountains have been gathered, so that the flocks may find pastures that satisfy them.

27.24.2.en: It is as though he says to the shepherds that there is a time when food is provided to the animals in the fold, and a time when we let them out in it to graze in the green pastures. So a man does not leave his animals without care.

27.24.3.en: This concerns the care of sheep; how much more is it fitting for us to care for the shepherding of souls, for we must serve them and so offer them the word of God as into their mouths, and go out with them onto the high mountains so that they may experience the heavenly life.

27.24.4.en: The Good Shepherd came down to our earth as to our fold, and carries us on His shoulders to lift us up to His heavens.

27.24.5.en: * There is nothing dearer to me than you, no, not even the light! I would gladly give my eyes tens of thousands of times and more, if possible, for the return of your souls!

27.24.6.en: Your salvation is very dear to me, more than the light itself...

27.24.7.en: For what use to me are the rays of the sun if sorrow darkens my eyes because of you...?

27.24.8.en: What hope would I have if you do not advance?

27.24.9.en: And on the contrary, what despair could come upon me as long as you are growing? For when I hear joyful news about you, I seem like one who has wings... Fulfill my joy...

27.24.10.en: I love you, until I melt in you, and you are to me everything, my father and my mother and my brothers and my children.

27.25.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The lambs are for thy clothing, and the price of a field is the he-goats [26].

27.25.1.en: When a person cares for his sheep and practices his love for them, he also receives a reward, for he says: “The lambs are for thy clothing,” that is, he uses the wool of the sheep to make the clothes he wears. And some of the wool remains, which he sells, and from it he gives the owner of the field as a wage.

27.26.0.en: And thou shalt have goats’ milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and for the maintenance for thy maidens [27].

27.26.1.en: The man who is faithful in his work, even if it is tending sheep, finds for himself and for all the members of his household the clothing they need, and food, and all their livelihood in abundance.

27.26.2.en: Grant me faithfulness, O Faithful One!

27.26.3.en: * Grant me faithfulness in my time, so that I count today as my treasure, and the present moment as my capital.

27.26.4.en: I do not grieve over the past that has gone by.

27.26.5.en: Nor do I rely on the future which is not in my hand.

27.26.6.en: * Let me be faithful in my depths.

27.26.7.en: You have covered me by Your love, so let me not exploit Your love and seek praise that is not my right.

27.26.8.en: Scatter all pride that arises from my depths.

27.26.9.en: * The wrath of fools is heavy and crushing, but You call me to bear the burdens of my own soul.

27.26.10.en: There is none to save me and uphold me but You!

27.26.11.en: * Let me be faithful to my friends.

27.26.12.en: Let me hear their criticism with largeness of heart and a longing for edification.

27.26.13.en: And if I criticize, let it be in a spirit of constructive love.

27.26.14.en: Faithful are the wounds of a lover.

27.26.15.en: And deceitful are the kisses of an enemy.

27.26.16.en: * Let me possess You, O Faithful One, so that my depths may be satisfied with You, and I may trample the honey of this world and all its desires.

27.26.17.en: Let me hunger for You and not for the world, so that I find sweetness in the fellowship of Your sufferings, and bitterness in trivial pleasures.

27.26.18.en: * Embrace me with my loved ones in You, so that the fragrant scent of Your sweet aroma may be diffused among us, and accept our love for one another as a joyful incense, and grant us heavenly sweetness and heavenly counsel.

27.26.19.en: * Grant me wisdom in every action, so that Your heart may rejoice in Your work in me.

27.26.20.en: Let me walk as is fitting with my neighbor, and enjoy Your peace in my house.

27.26.21.en: And let me benefit from fellowship with my brethren * You are my satisfaction, in You I find my rest and my peace.

27.26.22.en: In You I find every glory that I desire.

27.26.23.en: In You I work faithfully, and I remain working until I meet You!

28.0.0.en: 1 The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a steadfast young lion. 2 For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged.

28.0.1.en: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a steadfast young lion [1].

28.0.2.en: The wicked man suffers from a hidden inner enemy, namely the sense of guilt, even if he boasts of his evil and appears before others to be rejoicing and happy. He suffers from an inner persecutor who will not leave him wherever he is, even on his bed and in his dreams. This is what happened with our first parents, for when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden, they tried to hide from the face of the Lord, and Adam said: “I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself” (Gen 3:10). And when Cain killed his brother, he said to God in terror: “Every one that findeth me shall slay me” (Gen 14:14).

28.0.3.en: The Lord says of those who break the Law: “And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth. And they shall fall one upon another, as it were before a sword, when none pursueth: and ye shall have no power to stand before your enemies” (Lev 26:36-37). As it was said: “The LORD shall cause thee to be smitten before thine enemies: thou shalt go out one way against them, and flee seven ways before them: and shalt be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth” (Deut 28:25).

28.0.4.en: But the righteous, even if he sins, in a spirit of humility with reliance on God and hope in His love, sees his Savior dwelling at once in his heart, and is filled with strength.

28.0.5.en: Godliness in the Lord brings us into the blessed life and the experience of heavenly peace, whereas evil deprives a man of inner peace and stability, without any need for an outer enemy. Therefore it is fitting for us to enjoy not theoretical knowledge of goodness but practical experience, so that we sit with the Lord in the heavenly places.

28.0.6.en: * Many are the swords that pass through our land if we do not keep the law of the Lord and follow His commandments! Let each one enter into himself and contemplate his inner being, lest our land, that is our body, be stirred up by the spirit of fornication or troubled by the spirit of anger and agitation, or by the movement of avarice, or by the bow of lust and pleasures... The Apostle Paul knows this when he says: “Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor 10:5), so that we do not submit to this sword and these wars, but the Lord keeps our land in safety.

28.0.7.en: Origen * The knowledge of goodness is not enough to reach blessedness. Rather, goodness must be put into practice through works. Godliness in the Lord is in truth the beginning of knowledge.

28.0.8.en: St. Didymus the Blind * How does (the wicked) flee when no one pursues? This happens inwardly, where his conscience leads him as his own accuser and pursues him in every place. As he cannot flee from himself, so he cannot flee from his inner persecutor, but wherever he goes he is struck and wounded with a wound that cannot be healed. But the righteous is the opposite.

28.0.9.en: * Do you see the rock? Have you seen the sand, how the building sinks into it easily, and how it is easily affected by calamities? And how it is defeated? Although it is supported by property and the crowd and the nobles, it does not merely fall, but its fall is great. For He says: “and great was the fall of it” (Mt 7:27).

28.0.10.en: The danger is not in trivial matters, but in the loss of the soul, and the loss of heaven and the eternal blessings. And even before the loss there is no life more wretched than the life of a man who lives thus, in constant misery, and anxiety and disturbances and cares. This is what the wise man spoke of once, saying: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth” (Prov 28:1). For such people tremble even at the mere sight of their shadows, and suspect their friends and their enemies and their servants, those they know and those they do not know. Therefore before their final punishment they are punished here with severe punishment; for they refrain from carrying out the good and righteous commandments, deceived by the things of the present time, instead of fleeing from the life of vice. And it was fitting for them to flee from evil.

28.0.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * Lie down in rest without anxiety. Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet. Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it cometh” (Prov 3:24-25).

28.0.12.en: He said these words about the righteous and wise man... If you are righteous no one can frighten you. If you fear God you will not fear another. The righteous is like a lion who feels confidence in himself (cf. Prov 28:1). And according to the words of David: “Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night” (Ps 91:5), and so on. He adds also: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Ps 27:3). Do you not see the courage of the soul that keeps the commandments of God?

28.0.13.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * (The righteous) is not afraid of the things announced here, as it is written: “The righteous are bold as a lion” (cf. Prov 28:1), bold in everything by faith, not as one who tempts the Lord, but as one who trusts in the Holy Spirit. And since God is the subject of his constant concern, God will say to him: “I am with you in trouble, and I will deliver you and glorify you.”

28.1.0.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged [2].

28.1.1.en: He speaks here of the lands in which cases of rebellion and revolt against the rulers are many. For the multiplication of revolutions leads to the ruin of the kingdom. But if there is found a wise leader with understanding and knowledge, he gives the country some stability, and the people find rest in him. This applies to every society, especially church communities, for they are in need of spiritual leaders marked by love, calm and meekness, to win everyone as far as possible, and to gather all in a spirit of love and unity.

28.1.2.en: * O teacher, steward of the divine mysteries, speak with love.

28.1.3.en: He who teaches and does not love is restrained by silence, for he labors in vain composing unprofitable words.

28.1.4.en: The great skilled one, if he wishes to win his hearers, let him love much and speak little with his disciples.

28.2.s.en: 2. The poor man who oppresses his brother

28.2.0.en: A poor man that oppresseth the poor is like a sweeping rain which leaveth no food [3].

28.2.1.en: Sometimes a poor man receives authority, and he does not remember what he suffered in the days of his poverty and show compassion to his poor brethren, but treats the poor worse than others treat them. Such a man is like the sweeping rain which, instead of helping the seeds to grow, sweeps them away, destroying the soil of his heart as well as the soil of others.

28.2.2.en: When the Lord Christ wanted to give an example of showing compassion to others, to remind us that we are poor and in need of the mercies of God, so that we may show compassion to our poor and afflicted brethren, He said: “Therefore is the kingdom of heaven likened unto a certain king, which would take account of his servants. And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents. But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. The servant therefore fell down, and worshipped him, saying, Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt. But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest. And his fellowservant fell down at his feet, and besought him, saying, Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. And he would not: but went and cast him into prison, till he should pay the debt. So when his fellowservants saw what was done, they were very sorry, and came and told unto their lord all that was done. Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” (Mt 18:23-33).

28.2.3.en: * While the voice of forgiveness was still ringing in his ears, he forgot the compassionate love of his master! See what a good thing it is to remember your sins! For if this man had kept them clearly in his memory he would not have become so cruel and violent. Therefore I repeat... that the remembrance of our transgressions is exceedingly useful and very necessary. Nothing makes the soul truly wise and gentle and compassionate like the constant remembrance of our sins. For this reason Paul remembered the sins he had committed, not only after purification, but those which he had committed before his baptism, although all of these had been forgiven at once and removed.

28.2.4.en: * Do you not see the mercy of the Lord? Do you not see, on the contrary, the lack of mercy of the servant... even the gesture of supplication (of his fellow servant toward him) did not remind him of the gentleness of his master. In his greed he removed all this from his mind, and with violence and malice became more savage than any beast of prey, for he seized him by the throat... He had received complete pardon, while the other asked of him a postponement, and he did not give it to him, but cast him into prison.

28.3.0.en: 4 They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the law contend with them. 5 Evil men understand not the truth: but they that seek the LORD understand all things. 6 Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich. 7 Whoso keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that is a companion of the prodigal shameth his father. 8 He that by usury and increase multiplieth his wealth, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor. 9 He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.

28.3.1.en: They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the law contend with them [4].

28.3.2.en: What occupies the minds of wicked, unjust judges and men of authority is not obedience to the divine commandment and walking according to the Law, but the calming of their consciences. They support the wicked who walk as they do, practicing injustice, reckoning that their happiness lies in enjoying temporal things, whatever their source, and regardless of the means. But those who love God find their delight and enjoyment in the divine commandment; they reject injustice, and do not justify the conduct of the unjust but rebuke them.

28.3.3.en: * The Stoics base their teachings on the premise that the goal is to enjoy life (pleasures) according to nature, using the word “nature” in an improper way instead of the word “God,” since nature belongs to plants and crops and trees and stones. In any case the phrase is clear: “The base never think of the law, but the lovers of the law stand before them like a wall.” For the wisdom of capable men understands the ways of wisdom, but the folly of fools walks in a wrong direction.

28.4.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Evil men understand not the truth: but they that seek the LORD understand all things [5].

28.4.1.en: The wicked do not understand the truth, since they do not experience it in practice, even if they are members of the Catholic Church and have a visible role in it. But he who seeks the Lord and fears Him walks with wisdom and understanding. As the Apostle says: “Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things... yet he himself is judged of no man” (1 Cor 2:12, 15).

28.4.2.en: Evil corrupts the inner insight and covers the mind with the fog of ignorance, but the righteousness of Christ grants understanding and wisdom and learning and knowledge.

28.4.3.en: * Those who walk in a wicked life, even if they are members of the Catholic Church, must hasten to stop this wicked life before they depart from this life, and let them bear in mind that the name “Catholic” is not enough for salvation... For in the book of Proverbs everyone is commanded to fear the Lord and depart from evil. For it was said in it: [“Fear the Lord, and depart from evil; it shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones”] (cf. Prov 3:7-8).

28.4.4.en: Fulgentius * As it is written: “In thy light shall we see light,” that is, by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, “the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world”... so that the glory of the Only-Begotten Son appears, and He grants the knowledge of God to the true worshippers.

28.4.5.en: * It is very important for us not to devote ourselves ignorantly to the sciences, but to know which of them is the most beneficial... And for fear that we become attached to them and forget the knowledge of God, immersed in vain researches, he shows that it is necessary to use discernment in education, in such a way that we choose the useful knowledge and avoid everything that is harmful and ill-omened.

28.5.0.en: St. Basil the Great Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich [6].

28.5.1.en: Some think that poverty is a sign of God’s wrath against a man, and that wealth and abundance of goods are a sign of God’s favor. But there are holy poor who walk in uprightness like Lazarus (in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man), while the rich man was wicked.

28.5.2.en: What commends us before God is neither our wealth nor our poverty, neither our temporal honor nor our disgrace in the eyes of men, nor the spiritual or temporal standing of our ancestors, but our fellowship with God and our passionate love for the divine commandment.

28.5.3.en: * True nobility is not in the loftiness of the standing of ancestors, but in the goodness of your own character. Do not tell me that my father is a governor; what does that matter...? Even if your father were St. Paul, even if your brothers were martyrs, but you do not resemble them in their goodness, kinship will not profit you. Rather, it will harm you and condemn you. One of you may say that my mother is a benefactress who donates money. What does this profit you while you are in this cruelty of yours? Her kindness to men is an accusation added to the list of your sins. What did John the Baptist say to the Jews? “Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father” (Lk 3:8).

28.5.4.en: Is one of your ancestors a glorified saint (a cause for boasting)? If you resemble him you gain, but if you do not resemble him, this good ancestor becomes your accuser, because you will be a bitter fruit of a good tree. Never think that he who has a righteous relative is fortunate, if his conduct does not resemble the conduct of this good relative. Is your mother wicked? This has nothing to do with you (it does not affect you), just as the goodness of a godly mother will not profit you at all if you do not resemble her.

28.5.5.en: Likewise the evils of a bad (unrighteous) mother will not harm you if you take a different course for your life. Just as in the world to come you will deserve much blame because you had a good example within your house and did not imitate it, so also the person who has an unrighteous mother and did not resemble her in her evils will deserve a great reward, because he is a good ripe fruit from a bitter trunk.

28.5.6.en: Therefore it is not the loftiness of the standing of your ancestors, but the goodness of your own person that you need; for my part, I consider even the slave a noble man, and the master bound in chains, if I know the qualities of his character. And the person of high station belongs to the lowest class if he has the qualities of slavery. For who is truly and in fact the slave if not the person who commits iniquities? As for the other slavery, it is nothing but a matter of our outward circumstances. But this slavery consists of the passions of our impulses.

28.6.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Whoso keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that is a companion of the prodigal shameth his father [7].

28.6.1.en: He who keeps the divine commandment experiences the sweetness of God his Father’s love for him, but he who does not care about the fatherhood of his Father, and squanders his money on pleasures and lusts as the prodigal son did (Lk 15), grieves the heart of his father.

28.7.0.en: He that by usury and increase multiplieth his wealth, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor! [8].

28.7.1.en: Greed is hateful to God, for he who lends to his needy brother, not for trade or establishing projects, but for living, and demands interest, God often leaves him for a time, and his wealth is transferred in one way or another to a man who has pity on the poor. He gathers and stores up and does not know for whom he leaves it. As the psalmist says: “Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them” (Ps 39:6). Greed tries to gather for itself whatever it can and by every means, and does not realize that his soul may be required of him on that very day, or that he may lose all his possessions, while the poor may become rich. Time passes quickly so that all stand before God, and wealth does not intercede for its owner.

28.7.2.en: * “The rich man also died, and was buried”... Do not pass lightly over this phrase... “and was buried.”

28.7.3.en: My beloved, tables inlaid with silver and couches and carpets and costly clothes and the other various kinds of furnishings and perfumed oils and delicacies and large quantities of aged wines, and large quantities of food and costly table utensils, and flatterers and guards and servants and all the displays of pomp and show, fade and wither... All things are dust and ashes, sad melodies and mourning, for no one can offer help after it is too late, or bring back the soul that has departed. Then you will experience the power of gold and excessive wealth, for from among the crowd of those present he was taken naked and alone, and could not take with him anything of his abundant riches, but was taken without a companion or helper. None of those who used to serve him could rescue him from punishment and retribution, but he departed far from his retinue, for he was taken away by himself, to bear the unbearable torment: “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:6-8).

28.7.4.en: Truly death came and extinguished all this luxury and led him away as a captive with bowed head, groaning in shame, unable to speak, trembling in fear, as though his enjoyment of all this luxury had been a dream.

28.7.5.en: * The present world is a theater, and the conditions of men are roles they play, rich and poor, ruler and ruled, and so it is when this day ends and this terrible night comes. What a day it is, a pitch-black night for sinners, but a brilliant day for the righteous. When the play ends, and the masks are removed, when each one is judged according to his works, and not according to his wealth, or his office, or his position, or his power, but each one according to his works, whether ruler or king, lady or man. So when we are asked to give account of our lives and of our good works, do not say that our standing or the lowliness of our poverty will have any effect.

28.8.0.en: St. John Chrysostom He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination [9].

28.8.1.en: The Holy One inclines His ears to hear the prayers of His children issuing from an upright heart and a sincere intention, before they utter them with their tongues. But as for those who are set on their evil without repentance, He does not accept their sacrifices, nor does He answer their prayers. God says: “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats... incense is an abomination unto me... yea, when ye make many prayers, I will not hear: your hands are full of blood” (Isa 1:11-15). As the psalmist says: “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Ps 66:18).

28.8.2.en: * The Scripture says: “He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.” Why then are we astonished if God is slow to listen to our petitions, if we on our part are slow to hear the commandment of God, or do not care for it at all?

28.8.4.en: * It is fitting for us to read what is written in the book of Solomon with great attention and fear, and not with indifference. “He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.” It is fitting for a person first to desire to listen to God, if he wants God to listen to him. Truly with what boldness does a man want God to listen to him, if he despises God so much as to refuse to listen to His commandments? How is this, my brethren? Some Christians, and what is worse, even priests at times, when they prepare to make a journey, get ready bread and wine and oil and everything they need, and while they make huge preparations for their earthly journeys so that their bodies may live, is not one of them concerned to read one book to refresh his soul here and there?

28.8.5.en: * We must fear utterly what the Lord says by the prophet: “Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge” (Isa 5:13). Moreover: “He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law of the Lord, even his prayer shall be abomination” (cf. Prov 28:9).

28.8.6.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Let there be a zeal of love in prayer, then the effective answer of the one who hears it is realized.

28.8.7.en: * If you knock with godly love and sincere heartfelt love, He sees your motive for knocking, and opens to you.

28.8.8.en: * The cry to God is not made with a bodily voice, but with the heart. Many have silent lips, yet they cry out with the heart, and many offer noise with their lips, while their hearts have become unable to offer anything. Therefore if you cry to God, cry to Him from within, where He hears you.

28.9.0.en: 10 Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit: but the perfect shall have good things in possession. 11 The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out. 12 When righteous men do rejoice, there is great glory: but when the wicked rise, a man is hidden. 13 He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. 14 Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief. 15 As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people. 16 The prince that wanteth understanding is also a great oppressor: but he that hateth covetousness shall prolong his days.

28.9.1.en: Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit.

28.9.2.en: But the perfect shall have good things in possession [10].

28.9.3.en: Leading the upright astray or causing them to stumble is the work of the devil and his hosts, so he who practices this work becomes an ambassador of Satan, and his work is very hateful to God. Balaam gave counsel to the king of Moab to make the people of God fall into fornication, so that God would forsake them (Rev 2:14; Num 31:16).

28.9.4.en: “The perfect,” that is, “the blameless,” receive good from the hand of the Lord.

28.9.5.en: * Do everything with gentleness and order for edification. You must choose the person and the time and the need and the place as is fitting, and be firm in that. For when you take all these details into account you avoid every shadow of an evil effect.

28.9.6.en: * Be no stumbling block by any means to those you meet. Be cheerful to those you meet. Be cheerful, loving of the brethren, gentle and humble. Do not offend against the purpose of hospitality by asking for excessive food.

28.10.0.en: St. Basil the Great The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out [11].

28.10.1.en: Wealth often drives the rich man to conceit and pride, so he justifies his injustice to others and his stinginess toward his poor brethren, and ascribes wisdom to himself. But the godly poor man exposes the self-deception of the proud rich man, remembering the Lord’s saying to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked... anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see” (Rev 3:17-18).

28.11.0.en: When righteous men do rejoice, there is great glory: but when the wicked rise, a man is hidden [12].

28.11.1.en: When the righteous prosper many rejoice, because the prosperity of the righteous is for the edification of the community. But the success of the wicked, and their assuming leadership positions, causes a state of terror and frustration in the souls of the people, for fear of their evil plots.

28.11.2.en: This is what happened in the days of the prophet Elijah when the wicked Ahab and his wife Jezebel took the kingship; the prophets and the righteous disappeared, so that Elijah thought that he alone was left worshipping the Lord (1 Kgs 19:10, 14).

28.12.0.en: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy [13].

28.12.1.en: The sinning man tends to justify himself and not to confess his fault, as our first parents Adam and Eve did, and indeed the sinner sometimes puts the blame on the circumstances around him, and sometimes on God Himself. God has asked us to confess our sins, as the prophet David confessed before the prophet Nathan (2 Sam 12:13). And the people came to the Jordan and were baptized by John the Baptist, confessing their sins (Mt 3:6; Mk 1:5). And St. John the Apostle says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 Jn 1:9).

28.12.2.en: * He who is wounded in war is not ashamed to hand himself over to the hand of a wise physician, because he was overcome and wounded. And when he is healed, the king does not reject him but counts him with his army. So it is fitting for the man whom Satan has wounded not to be ashamed to confess his follies, and to depart from them, seeking repentance as medicine for his soul.

28.12.3.en: For he who is ashamed to show his wound, the harm extends to his whole body.

28.12.4.en: He who is not ashamed of this has his wound healed, and returns to the battle.

28.12.5.en: St. Aphrahat * The sinner who confesses his sins and says: [“My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness”] (cf. Ps 38:5), his loathsome wounds are taken away from him, and he becomes clean in health. But he who covers his sins shall not prosper.

28.12.6.en: St. Jerome * “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Prov 28:13).

28.12.7.en: He who thinks that he hides his guilt perishes in empty hope, because that is mere feeble talk and not the truth. Truly “the talk of sinners is hateful in vain” (Sir 27:13), it gives no fruit but only wailing! For “the talk of a fool is like a burden in the way” (Sir 21:16). And what is sin but a weight? A weight on the shoulder of one passing through this world, so that he is weighed down with a heavy load of guilt! If he wishes not to be subject to carrying the weight, he must turn to the Lord who said: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28)...

28.12.8.en: What misery could be greater than this? For even the bed, which gives all people rest, causes terrible pain. And then we truly remember what we have done, and our inner conscience is pricked by the goads of its own deeds. For what reason does the Holy Bible say to such people: “Commune with your own heart upon your bed” (Ps 4:4), “what you say in your hearts, repent of it upon your beds”?

28.12.9.en: This is truly the remedy for sin, but the conscience is still wounded!

28.12.10.en: * “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Prov 28:13).

28.12.11.en: In truth the wise man moves toward repentance for his errors, but the fool finds pleasure in them. “The righteous man is his own accuser” (Prov 18:17), but the wicked defends himself. The righteous wants to be ahead of his accuser in mentioning his sins, but the wicked wants to hide them. One rushes at the beginning of his speech to reveal his sin, and the other tries to remove the accusation from himself by the chatter of his speech, like one who does not reveal his sin.

28.13.0.en: St. Ambrose Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief [14].

28.13.1.en: The godly man, or he in whom is the fear of the Lord, enjoys the blessed life, for he delights in heavenly wisdom. But he who turns his back to God and does not carry in him the fear of the Lord carries in him a spirit of violence and cruelty.

28.13.2.en: * He who fears (is godly toward) the Lord keeps away from error, and directs his ways to the path of virtue. Apart from the man who fears the Lord, man is unable to renounce sin.

28.13.3.en: St. Ambrose * Let your petitions be spiritual... let your mind be watchful, let your concerns be centered on the (divine) words. Ask for the things that are fitting to ask of God, and you will receive what you ask. For the same purpose be careful to keep constant vigil, watchfulness, your care not darkened, your mind not wavering in one direction and another, but working out your salvation with fear and trembling. The Scripture says: “Happy is the man that feareth alway.”

28.13.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * Work diligently in the soil that is yours. Turn over your land with the plow. Cast the stones far from your field, and root out the thorns. Be unwilling to have the hard heart that makes the word of God ineffective (Ps 95:8; Mk 16:14). Be unwilling to have a thin layer of soil where divine love finds no depth to enter.

28.13.5.en: St. Augustine * He who in everything stands in fear out of a blessed and dignified modesty, and abides in the truth, since he can say: “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Ps 16:8).

28.14.0.en: * The souls with whom you wish to speak wisely must first be purified by the fear of God. For he who distributes the mysteries of salvation to the public, and receives all persons alike, including those who have not been adorned with purity, and have not been tested and qualified to use the mysteries properly, is like one who pours very precious ointment into filthy vessels. St. Basil the Great As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people [15].

28.14.1.en: The leader who has no understanding of true love turns from tender fatherhood into a roaring lion that wishes to devour, and a bear that rages without cause. He devours the poor and crushes the weak, instead of being an ambassador of the Lord Christ, the Lover of mankind, and imitates the devil, the murderer of men from the beginning. But the loving leader carries the spirit of the Lord Christ who gave Himself.

28.14.2.en: * You must join meekness to bodily labor. For it is not enough for you to toil much, but you must do it with gentleness. And steep your speech in meekness and tenderness. Let others know that you do all your work in a spirit of love, and so they will be most pleased by your service. And the wise man teaches you this when he says: “My son, blame not when thou doest good, and use not hard words when thou givest any thing. Shall not the dew assuage the heat? so is a word better than a gift.”

28.14.3.en: St. Basil the Great * “Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me...? Feed my sheep” (Jn 21).

28.14.4.en: May we not love ourselves but love Him, and in shepherding His sheep seek what is His and not what is ours, for he who can live by himself will surely die if he loves himself. And by this he is not a lover of himself, for by loving himself he loses his life.

28.14.5.en: May the shepherds of the flock not be lovers of themselves, lest they shepherd the flock as though it were their own property and not the flock of Christ.

28.14.6.en: For they seek material gain as “lovers of money,” or lord it over the people as “boasters,” or seek glory from the honor offered to them as “proud,” or fall into heresies as “blasphemers,” and despise the holy Fathers as “disobedient to parents,” and return evil for good to those who desire to reform them lest they perish as “unthankful,” and kill their own souls and the souls of others as those “without mercy,” and try to distort the characters of the saints as “false witnesses,” and give free rein to base lusts as “unholy,” and complain always... as “implacable,” and know nothing of the service of love as those “without natural affection,” and trouble mankind with their foolish discussions as “headstrong,” and do not understand what they say or what they insist upon as “blind,” and prefer bodily pleasures to spiritual joy as “lovers of their own selves more than lovers of God.”
